objective: By the end of this lesson you can show you meet the commercial pilot requirements, and decide for any flight whether you may act as pilot in command for pay: the right certificate, limitation, endorsements, currency, second-class medical and documents, and whether the operation itself is legal.
why: The commercial certificate lets you be paid to fly, but it does not make every paid flight legal. Many new commercial pilots get in trouble not with their flying, but by taking a job that needed an operator certificate, a newer medical, or an endorsement they did not have.

warmup: You just passed your commercial checkride. A friend of a friend sees your post and offers you $500 to fly his family 200 NM to a wedding on Friday night in a rented airplane. You are commercial, so you can be paid to fly, right? List everything you would want to check before you answer.

key_terms.def: Being paid, in money or anything else of value, for flying. A commercial pilot may act as PIC for compensation or hire if qualified under the parts that apply to the operation (14 CFR 61.133).

A person who, for compensation or hire, carries persons or property by aircraft, other than as an air carrier. The test: is the flying merely incidental to another business, or a major enterprise for profit in itself? (14 CFR 1.1)
Offering to the public to fly for compensation or hire. The FAA weighs it when deciding if a flight is a commercial operation, such as a commercial air tour (14 CFR 93.303).
Placed on a commercial airplane certificate when the pilot has no instrument rating: carrying passengers for hire on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night is prohibited (14 CFR 61.133(b)).
An airplane with retractable landing gear, flaps, and a controllable pitch propeller (or FADEC).
For commercial training: an airplane with a PFD, an MFD with a GPS moving map, and a two-axis autopilot tied to the navigation and heading guidance (14 CFR 61.129(j)).
An airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower. PIC needs training and a one-time endorsement.
The minimum medical to exercise commercial pilot privileges. Good for commercial privileges through the end of the 12th month after the exam month, at any age.
What an operator of nonstop passenger flights for hire (same airport, within 25 statute miles) must get from Flight Standards under 14 CFR 91.147.
For commercial aeronautical experience, a flight with a landing more than 50 NM straight-line from the original departure point, using navigation to get there.

chunks.title: Who can earn the commercial certificate

body.p: To be eligible for a commercial pilot certificate you must meet every item in [[60:310|14 CFR 61.123]]. Compare it with what you did for private:

head: Requirement
Private (61.103)
Commercial (61.123)
rows: Endorsement, then pass the commercial test (61.125 areas)
At least a private pilot certificate

body.p: The commercial knowledge areas start with the regulations for commercial privileges, limitations and flight operations, and NTSB accident reporting [[60:310|14 CFR 61.125(b)(1)-(2)]]. Training for commercial focuses on a better understanding of aircraft systems and a higher standard of airmanship [[1:33|PHAK 1-18]].

callout.text: You only need a third-class medical to take the commercial practical test [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)(iii)]]. But you need a second-class medical the moment you want to use your new commercial privileges [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]].

body.p: Like your private certificate, the commercial certificate has no expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(c)(1)]]. What expires is your medical and your currency.

check.q: You are 17 and have 260 hours. Can you take the commercial practical test?
check.a: No. You must be at least 18 years old to be eligible [[60:310|14 CFR 61.123(a)]].

body.p: For a commercial certificate with airplane single-engine, you must log at least 250 hours of flight time as a pilot, made up of at least the items below [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)]].

head: Requirement (minimum)
Amount
rows: 100 hours, incl. 50 in airplanes and 50 cross-country (10 of the cross-country in airplanes)
20 hours, which include the five items below
10 hours, 5 of them in a single-engine airplane
10 hours, in any mix of those airplanes
One 2-hour flight, more than 100 NM straight-line from the departure point
One 2-hour flight, more than 100 NM straight-line from the departure point
3 hours with an instructor within the 2 calendar months before the test month
Solo or PIC duties with instructor on board
10 hours, incl. the long cross-country and night items below
300 NM total, landings at 3 points, one point at least 250 NM straight-line from departure
5 hours with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings (each with a traffic pattern) at a towered airport

callout.text: New since private: the 10 hours of solo can be 10 hours of performing PIC duties with an instructor on board, and those hours may also count toward the 100 hours of PIC time [[60:315|14 CFR 61.129(a)(4)]].

body.p: What counts as cross-country here is stricter than for logging in general: for commercial aeronautical experience the flight must include a landing more than 50 NM straight-line from the original departure point, and use navigation to get there [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1, cross-country time (ii)]].

Simulator credit: if you did not train in a Part 142 course, you may credit at most 50 hours toward the 250, and only time with an authorized instructor in a full flight simulator or flight training device that represents the class of airplane [[60:320|14 CFR 61.129(i)(1)(i)]]. In a Part 142 course the cap is 100 hours, and finishing an approved Part 142 commercial course lets 190 hours meet the total [[60:320|14 CFR 61.129(i)(2)(i)]], [[60:321|61.129(i)(3)]].

check.q: Your long cross-country goes 310 NM total with 3 landings, but the farthest airport is 230 NM straight-line from home. Does it count?
check.a: No. One landing point must be at least 250 NM straight-line from the original departure point [[60:315|14 CFR 61.129(a)(4)(i)]].

chunks.title: Complex, TAA and high-performance: training and endorsements

body.p: The 10 hours of advanced-airplane training may be in a complex airplane, a turbine airplane, or a technically advanced airplane (TAA), or any mix [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(ii)]]. To count as a TAA, the airplane must have all of these installed [[60:321|14 CFR 61.129(j)]]:

bullets: An electronic primary flight display (PFD) with at least airspeed, turn coordinator, attitude, heading, altimeter and vertical speed.
An electronic multifunction display (MFD) with at least a GPS moving map showing the airplane's position.
A two-axis autopilot integrated with the navigation and heading guidance system.
The PFD and MFD elements must be continuously visible.

body.p: On a panel like this, the PFD is the screen in front of the left seat, and the MFD is the second screen near the center [[23:149|IFH 6-16]].
Training time and endorsements are two different things. These are the 61.31 rules for acting as PIC:

head: Airplane
Definition
To act as PIC
rows: Retractable gear, flaps, and controllable pitch propeller (or FADEC) [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]]
Ground and flight training plus a one-time endorsement [[60:213|61.31(e)]]
Ground and flight training plus a one-time endorsement [[60:213|61.31(f)]], [[60:214|61.31(f)(1)(ii)]]
No 61.31 endorsement; a thorough checkout is strongly recommended [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.1]]

callout.text: A glass-cockpit, fixed-gear airplane can count toward your 10 hours of TAA training and still need a high-performance endorsement if its engine is over 200 HP. Check each rule on its own.

check.q: A fixed-gear airplane has a 180 HP engine, a PFD, an MFD with a GPS moving map, and a two-axis autopilot tied to the GPS and heading. Which 61.31 endorsement do you need to act as PIC?
check.a: None of the complex or high-performance endorsements: the gear is fixed [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]] and 180 HP is not more than 200 HP [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]. It does meet the TAA definition, so it counts toward the 10 hours of training [[60:321|14 CFR 61.129(j)]].

chunks.title: Commercial privileges and the no-instrument limitation

body.p: A commercial pilot may act as PIC of an aircraft carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, and may act as PIC for compensation or hire. Both privileges come with a condition: the pilot must be qualified under Part 61 and under the other parts of the regulations that apply to the operation [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]].

head: Private pilot
Commercial pilot
rows: No, except the listed exceptions (business-incidental, charity events, search, sales demos, towing) [[60:307|61.113(a)]], [[60:308|61.113(b)-(h)]]
Yes, if qualified under the parts that apply to the operation [[60:322|61.133(a)(1)]]
Carry passengers or property for hire

body.p: If you earn a commercial airplane certificate without an instrument rating in the same category and class, your certificate will say: "The carriage of passengers for hire in airplanes on cross-country flights in excess of 50 nautical miles or at night is prohibited." It comes off when you meet the instrument rating requirements of 61.65 [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(b)(1)]].
Limitations like this one are printed on the back of your certificate, under XIII LIMITATIONS [[1:31|PHAK 1-16]].

callout.text: Read the limitation word by word. It is about passengers, for hire, on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night. A paid flight with no passengers is not covered by it. A free flight with a friend is not covered by it. Your instrument rating removes it.

Your commercial certificate is not an instructor certificate. Only a flight instructor with the right rating may give the training required for solo, endorse a pilot for a certificate or rating, or endorse a logbook for training given [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(d)(2)]].

body.p: You still need an instrument rating, and instrument currency, to act as PIC under IFR or in weather below VFR minimums [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)]].

check.q: You hold a commercial certificate with no instrument rating. May you fly a paying passenger 35 NM to another airport in daylight?
check.a: The 61.133(b)(1) limitation does not stop it: the flight is under 50 NM and not at night [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(b)(1)]]. You must still be qualified under the parts that apply to that operation [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]].

chunks.title: Pilot for hire versus operator: what is a commercial operation?

body.p: This is the biggest new idea at the commercial level. Your certificate lets you be paid as a pilot. It does not, by itself, let you sell air transportation to the public. Those are two different jobs.

The regulations define a commercial operator as a person who, for compensation or hire, carries persons or property by aircraft in air commerce, other than as an air carrier. When it is doubtful whether an operation is for compensation or hire, the test is whether the carriage by air is merely incidental to the person's other business, or is in itself a major enterprise for profit [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]].

Rules for companies that carry people and property for pay sit in their own part of 14 CFR, Subchapter G, Air Carriers and Operators for Compensation or Hire [[1:23|PHAK 1-8]]. Charter flights under Part 135 are run by a Part 119 certificate holder, which even has its own pilot certificate check plan [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)(v)]].

Holding out means offering to the public to fly for pay. The FAA lists a holding out to the public as one factor when it decides whether a sightseeing flight is a commercial air tour [[60:693|14 CFR 93.303]]. A post saying "I'll fly you anywhere, $200 an hour" is an offer to the public, not a favor for a friend.
Two kinds of passenger flights for pay have their own Part 91 rules. Compare them:

head: 91.146 charity, nonprofit or community event
91.147 nonstop flights for compensation or hire
rows: Nonstop, begin and end at the same airport, within 25 statute miles
Nonstop, begin and end at the same airport, within 25 statute miles
Sponsor sends a letter to Flight Standards at least 7 days before
Operator gets a Letter of Authorization from Flight Standards
Up to 30 passenger seats, 7,500 lb payload; private pilot PIC needs 500 hours
Drug and alcohol testing program (Part 120), Part 136 safety rules, Part 5
Not subject to Part 119 certification if all conditions are met

callout.text: The question to ask before every paid flight: who is the operator, and what authority does that operator hold for this kind of flight? A 91.147 LOA covers nonstop flights from one airport within 25 statute miles [[60:463|14 CFR 91.147(a)]]. It does not cover a trip to another city.

check.q: A local operator holds a 91.147 Letter of Authorization. A tour customer asks you to fly her 60 NM to another airport for lunch instead. Is that covered?
check.a: No. The LOA covers nonstop passenger flights that begin and end at the same airport within 25 statute miles [[60:463|14 CFR 91.147(a)]]. A trip to another airport is a different operation.

chunks.title: Staying current: flight review, landings and IFR

body.p: The recent experience rules are the same for commercial pilots as for private pilots. Getting paid does not change them, but a lapse now affects your job, not just your weekend.

head: Rule
Requirement
Source
rows: 1 hour ground and 1 hour flight training, since the start of the 24th calendar month before the month you fly
3 takeoffs and 3 landings in the preceding 90 days, same category, class and type (if required); full stop in a tailwheel airplane
3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise, in the preceding 90 days
6 approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking courses within the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight
IFR lapsed over 6 more calendar months
Only an instrument proficiency check restores it

callout.text: Your commercial checkride counts as a flight review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)(1)]]. Pass it in March 2026 and you are covered through March 31, 2028.

body.p: Not current for passengers? You may act as PIC to get current under day VFR or day IFR, with no persons or property on board other than those needed for the flight [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(2)]].
Instrument currency can be kept in an airplane or in a full flight simulator, flight training device or aviation training device, or any mix of them [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(2)]].

check.q: Your last 3 full-stop night landings were 95 days ago. A charter customer wants a night flight. What must you do first?
check.a: Make 3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise, without passengers, before carrying anyone at night [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

body.p: You must record the training and experience you use to meet the requirements for a certificate, rating or flight review, and for recent experience [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(a)]]. For your commercial application, your logbook is your proof of all 250 hours.

bullets: Each entry: date, total time, departure and arrival points, aircraft type and identification, and safety pilot name if one was required [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(1)]].
Type of experience: solo, PIC, SIC, or training from an authorized instructor [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(2)]].
Conditions: day or night, actual instrument, or simulated instrument [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(b)(3)]].
Training time must be endorsed by the instructor, with a description of the lesson, its length, and the instructor's signature and certificate number [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]].

body.p: PIC time: you may log PIC when you are the sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft you are rated for, when you are the sole occupant, or when you act as PIC of an aircraft that needs more than one pilot [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(e)(1)(i)-(iii)]]. So a rated private pilot flying a training cross-country with an instructor may log it as both PIC and training received.

Solo time is only time when you are the sole occupant [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(d)]]. For instrument currency, log the location and type of each approach and the safety pilot's name if one was required [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].
You must present your pilot certificate, medical and logbook on reasonable request by the FAA, the NTSB or any federal, state or local law enforcement officer [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

callout.text: Moved? After 30 days from a change of permanent mailing address you may not use your certificate until you have notified the FAA Airman Certification Branch in writing [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

check.q: You fly a 2-hour night cross-country with your instructor for 61.129, and you are rated ASEL and on the controls the whole time. How may you log it?
check.a: As PIC, because you are the sole manipulator of an aircraft you are rated for [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(e)(1)(i)]], and as training received, endorsed by the instructor [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]], with night conditions recorded [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(b)(3)]].

chunks.title: Medical: second class and the step-down

body.p: To exercise the privileges of a commercial certificate in an airplane you must hold at least a second-class medical [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]]. A first-class medical also works. Medicals come from an aviation medical examiner (AME) [[1:424|PHAK 17-2]].

A medical expires at the end of the last day of a month counted from the month of the exam. The month depends on what privileges you use that day, and for private privileges, on your age at the exam [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]].

head: Your medical
Commercial privileges
Private privileges, under 40 at exam
Private privileges, 40 or older at exam

callout.text: Step-down example: age 45, second-class exam in March 2026. Commercial privileges through March 31, 2027. After that, private privileges only, through March 31, 2028.

body.p: So an "expired" second-class medical is often still a good medical for flying as a private pilot. It just stops covering anything you do as a commercial pilot.

check.q: You are 32. Your second-class exam was in May 2026. On June 15, 2027, may you fly a paid banner tow? May you fly your family for free?
check.a: Not the banner tow: for commercial privileges the medical ran out May 31, 2027 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]]. The family flight is fine on private privileges, good through May 31, 2031 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(ii)]].

body.p: A valid medical card does not make you fit today. You may not act as PIC or as a required crewmember while you know, or have reason to know, of a medical condition that would make you unable to meet the standards for the medical you need, or while taking medication or treatment that does so [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]. For commercial flying, that means second-class standards.
Alcohol and drugs: no acting as a crewmember [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]:

bullets: Within 8 hours after drinking any alcohol
While under the influence of alcohol
While using any drug that affects your faculties in any way contrary to safety
With an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater

body.p: Aftereffects of alcohol, such as dehydration and hangover, can be a hazard for longer than eight hours [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

callout.text: A motor vehicle action, such as a DUI conviction or a license suspension for alcohol or drugs, must be reported in writing to the FAA Civil Aviation Security Division within 60 days [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]]. Failing to report is itself grounds for suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(f)]].
IMSAFE before every paid flight: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

check.q: You took a cold medicine that makes you drowsy. Your second-class medical is current. Can you fly today's paid flight?
check.a: No. You may not act as a crewmember while using a drug that affects your faculties contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]], and you may not act as PIC with a medication that makes you unable to meet your medical standards [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)(2)]].

chunks.title: Documents you carry as a commercial pilot

body.p: To serve as a required pilot, these must be in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft:

bullets: Your pilot certificate (or temporary certificate) [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]]
A photo ID: driver's license, government ID, U.S. Armed Forces ID, passport, or another accepted ID [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]], [[60:189|61.3(a)(2)(v)-(vi)]]
The appropriate medical certificate [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]. For commercial privileges that is a second-class or first-class medical [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]].

callout.text: The driver's license in place of a medical (BasicMed) works only for student, recreational, private and flight instructor privileges under 61.113(i) [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiii)-(xiv)]]. It never covers a flight you fly as a commercial pilot.

body.p: Your logbook does not have to ride along, but you must present it on reasonable request [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]]. The carry rules in 61.51(i) are for student, sport and recreational pilots [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(2)-(4)]].

check.q: You have your commercial certificate, your passport and a third-class medical from last month. Can you fly a paid ferry flight today?
check.a: No. Commercial privileges need at least a second-class medical [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]]. Your passport is a fine photo ID [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)(iv)]].

body.p: BasicMed lets a private pilot act as PIC, or serve as a required flightcrew member, without an FAA medical certificate, using a U.S. driver's license and the Part 68 course and exam [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]]. The rule is written for student, recreational and private privileges, and flight instructor privileges [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(v), (vii)]].

BasicMed does not apply to the privileges of a commercial or ATP certificate. Those need a first- or second-class medical [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]]. A commercial pilot on BasicMed may still fly, but only the kind of flying a private pilot may do.

head: BasicMed item (current 14 CFR)
Value
rows: Exam by a State-licensed physician (with the FAA checklist)
FAA medical held at some point
After July 14, 2006; not suspended or revoked
Not more than 7 occupants and 12,500 lb max takeoff weight
At or below 18,000 ft MSL, at or below 250 KIAS, in the U.S. unless authorized

body.p: Sources: [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)]], [[60:308|61.113(i)(1)-(2)]]. Your logbook must hold the completed exam checklist and the course completion certificate [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].

callout.text: AC 68-1A (2017) still lists the old limits: 6 occupants, 6,000 lb, 5 passengers [[36:8|AC 68-1A 3.2]]. The current regulation says 7 occupants, 12,500 lb, 6 passengers [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. Use the regulation. The AC's line "You may not fly for compensation or hire" still matches the rule, because 61.113 is the private pilot section.

body.p: Under BasicMed you may not act as PIC while you know or have reason to know of any medical condition that would make you unable to fly the aircraft safely [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(b), (c)(2)]].

check.q: Your second-class medical expired for all uses, but you meet BasicMed. Can you fly a paid aerial photo flight?
check.a: No. BasicMed does not cover commercial pilot privileges; they need a first- or second-class medical [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]], [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]].

chunks.title: Risk: proficiency versus currency, when someone is paying

body.p: Currency asks: have you logged the minimum events the rules require? Proficiency asks: can you manage the conditions expected on this flight? If your six approaches were five months ago, you may be legal for IFR and still lack the proficiency to fly low ceilings safely [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

The FAA calls the 61.57 landing rules minimums. If your recent landings were all in light winds on long runways, get more practice in stronger winds or on short runways before carrying passengers in those conditions [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]].

Commercial flying adds a big hazard: external pressure. Pressure to get to a destination, or not to disappoint someone waiting, can affect your judgment, and pilots under external pressure sometimes fail to consider the other hazards [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. A paying customer, a boss and a schedule are all external pressures.

Raise your personal minimums for each added risk, such as a lack of currency, an unfamiliar airplane or "must meet" deadlines. Never lower them to complete a specific flight; decide on changes when you have time to think, not under pressure [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

callout.text: The RMH says it plainly: professional pilots live by the numbers. Written personal minimums make a no-go call easier to explain to the passengers who depend on your judgment [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

check.q: You are IFR current by one week and the client is impatient. Ceilings are at your personal minimum. What should you do?
check.a: Recognize that currency is not proficiency and that client pressure is an external pressure hazard [[30:23|RMH 3-5]], [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Do not lower your minimums to make the trip; delay or cancel [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

body.p: Commercial training often puts you in a new airplane: a complex trainer, a high-performance airplane, or a TAA. Accident data shows rates go up for pilots with little or no time in the type they fly. The FAA recommends a full checkout in each make and model [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

Moving up needs structured training. Transition to a complex or high-performance airplane should follow a ground and flight syllabus with a qualified instructor [[24:248|AFH 12-17]]. Moving down is just as risky: weather, headwinds and turbulence affect a low-performance airplane more, crosswind ability may be lower, and the avionics may be less capable [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10, 2]].
Retractable gear brings new errors. Pilots moving to these airplanes have [[24:248|AFH 12-17]]:

bullets: Forgotten to extend the gear
Retracted the gear by accident
Moved the gear handle but not checked gear position
Misused the emergency gear system
Retracted the gear too early on takeoff, or extended it too late

body.p: Use the checklist every time, lower the gear at the same point on downwind, and wait until you clear the runway before you touch any levers [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

Glass and autopilots: learn the systems before you fly, and get a thorough evaluation from an instructor who knows that airplane's automation [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.1]]. Fly by hand at times to keep your skills [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]]. If the automation does something you do not expect, reduce the level of automation, fly manually, and take time to sort it out [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

check.q: You trained in a G1000 TAA. Your first paid job is in an older airplane with analog gauges and no autopilot. Does the risk go down?
check.a: No. Moving down has its own challenges: different handling, less capable avionics, and more effect from weather [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10, 2]]. Get a checkout in that make and model [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: can I take this paid flight?

body.p: The examiner will hand you a scenario and ask if you may act as PIC under VFR. For a commercial checkride, add the pay questions. Work through it in this order:

head: Check
Question
Rule
rows: Commercial ASEL? Is there a no-instrument limitation, and does it bite?
Within 24 calendar months, or a checkride since?
3 in 90? Night full stops? IFR 6 calendar months?
Second class within 12 calendar months for commercial privileges?
Any condition, medication or alcohol issue?
Pilot certificate, photo ID, second-class medical?
Who is the operator? Is it incidental, a 91.146 or 91.147 flight, or does it need operator authority?

body.p: Common errors examiners see in these scenarios:

bullets: Saying "I'm commercial, so I can be paid" without asking who the operator is [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]].
Reading the no-instrument limitation as "no flying for hire at night." It covers carrying passengers for hire on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(b)(1)]].
Forgetting the second-class medical stops covering commercial privileges after 12 calendar months [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]].
Calling a fixed-gear, over-200 HP airplane complex. It is high-performance [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]].
Using BasicMed for a paid flight [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]].

callout.text: Answer with the rule and the reason. Then give the safety view: legal, but am I proficient, and is anyone pressuring me? [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]

check.q: Which check is new at the commercial level compared with the private checklist?
check.a: Check 8, the operation: who the operator is and what authority it holds, because your certificate only covers you as the pilot [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]], [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]]. Also the second-class medical timing [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]].

f1.caption: Figure 1-20. Front side (top) and back side (bottom) of an airman certificate issued by the FAA.
f1.alt: Front of a plastic FAA airman certificate showing name, address, nationality, date of birth, certificate number and date of issue, and the back showing a block for XII Ratings, a block for XIII Limitations, and the holder's signature line.

f2.caption: Figure 12-11. Landing gear handles and single and multiple light indictor.
f2.alt: A landing gear lever in a slot marked UP, OFF and DN, with an override trigger, a gear limit speed placard, and red and green indicator lights for the nose, left and right gear above it.

f3.caption: Figure 6-21. Primary flight display (PFD) and analog counterparts.
f3.alt: A glass cockpit panel. The left screen is a PFD with an airspeed tape on the left, attitude display in the center, altitude tape and vertical speed strip on the right, and a heading display at the bottom. Callouts link each part to the matching round analog instrument. A second, blank screen sits to the right, and three backup analog gauges are below.

f4.caption: Figure 6-22. Multifunction display (MFD).
f4.alt: The same glass cockpit panel with the right screen lit as a multifunction display: a moving map with colored weather returns and engine instrument strips on its left side.

f5.caption: Figure 12-16. Sample transition training syllabus.
f5.alt: A two-column table of three one-hour ground lessons (flight manual operations, line inspection, flight deck familiarization; loading, limitations, servicing, instruments, radio and special equipment, systems; performance section, cruise control, review) beside three one-hour flight lessons (maneuvers, takeoffs, landings and go-arounds; emergency operations, instrument control, radio and autopilot; short and soft-field takeoffs and landings, maximum performance operations).

f6.caption: Figure 2-9. Examples of additional safety margins from baseline personal minimums.
f6.alt: Color-coded PAVE table: Pilot (illness, medication, stress, fatigue, lack of currency) add at least 500 feet to ceiling; Aircraft (unfamiliar airplane or avionics) add at least 1/2 mile visibility; enVironment (unfamiliar airports, terrain) add at least 500 feet runway length; External pressures (must-meet deadlines, passenger pressure) subtract at least 5 knots from winds.

scenario.title: Your first paid job offers
scenario.setup: It is Tuesday, October 20, 2026. You passed your commercial ASEL checkride on March 12, 2026. You hold an instrument rating. You are 41, and your last medical was a second-class exam in August 2025. Two weeks ago you made 3 daytime landings in a Cessna 172; your last night full-stop landings were 100 days ago. You flew 6 approaches, holding and tracking in May 2026. Two offers arrive. Offer A: a local tour operator that holds a 91.147 Letter of Authorization wants you to fly 20-minute nonstop sightseeing flights from your home airport, staying within 10 statute miles, this Saturday in daylight, in its Cessna 182 (230 HP, fixed gear, glass panel and autopilot). You have no high-performance endorsement. Offer B: a stranger who saw your social media post offers $500 plus the rental for you to fly his family 200 NM to a wedding Friday night.

questions.q: Can you use your commercial privileges today?
questions.a: No. A second-class medical covers commercial privileges only through the end of the 12th month after the exam month, so yours ran out August 31, 2026 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]]. You need a new second-class (or first-class) medical before any paid flight. It is still good for private privileges through August 31, 2027, because you were 40 or older at the exam [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(iii)]].
Yes. The commercial checkride counts [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)(1)]], so you are covered through March 31, 2028 [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]].

questions.q: After a new medical, what else do you need for Offer A?
questions.a: A high-performance endorsement, with ground and flight training, because 230 HP is more than 200 HP [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]. Your 3 landings two weeks ago keep you day-current for passengers [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]]. The operator, not you, must hold the LOA, drug and alcohol program and Part 136 safety provisions [[60:463|14 CFR 91.147(b)]].

questions.q: If you had no instrument rating, would the 61.133(b) limitation stop Offer A?
questions.a: No. The tours are local, in daylight, and not cross-country flights over 50 NM, so the limitation does not apply [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(b)(1)]].

No. It is not a 91.147 flight, because it does not begin and end at the same airport within 25 statute miles [[60:463|14 CFR 91.147(a)]]. You would be the one selling the carriage of passengers for pay after offering it to the public [[60:693|14 CFR 93.303]], which is the work of a commercial operator, not just a pilot [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]]. Your certificate only covers flights where you are qualified under the parts that apply to the operation [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]]. You are also not night-current [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

questions.q: Once you are legal for Offer A, what risks remain?
questions.a: An unfamiliar, higher-performance airplane with glass and an autopilot, plus pressure from a paying operator and waiting passengers. Get a checkout from an instructor who knows that automation [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.1]], raise your personal minimums for the unfamiliar airplane and external pressures, and do not lower them on the day [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

skills.do: Given a scenario by the examiner, decide whether you may act as PIC under VFR, including for compensation or hire. Check certificate and any 61.133(b) limitation, endorsements, flight review, day and night passenger currency, second-class medical timing, fitness, documents, and whether the operation itself is authorized. Cite the rule for each answer and say whether the flight is also safe.
skills.practice: Run the 8-check list on your own logbook and medical today. Then have your CFI invent 5 job offers (tours, banner towing, ferry, charter for a friend, charity event) and answer each out loud with the rule numbers [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133]], [[60:463|91.147]], [[60:209|61.23(d)]], in under 2 minutes each.

quiz.q: What is the minimum age to be eligible for a commercial pilot certificate?
quiz.why: You must be at least 18 years old [[60:310|14 CFR 61.123(a)]]. 17 is the private pilot age.

quiz.q: Outside a Part 142 course, how much total flight time must a commercial ASEL applicant log?
options: 200 hours
250 hours
190 hours
1,500 hours
quiz.why: At least 250 hours of flight time as a pilot [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)]]. 190 hours applies only to an approved Part 142 commercial course [[60:321|14 CFR 61.129(i)(3)]].

quiz.q: The long solo (or PIC duties) cross-country for commercial ASEL must be:
options: 150 NM total with 3 landings, one leg over 50 NM
250 NM total with 2 landings
300 NM total, with one point at least 150 NM away
300 NM total, 3 landing points, one at least 250 NM straight-line from departure
quiz.why: Not less than 300 NM total, landings at a minimum of three points, one at least 250 NM straight-line from the original departure point [[60:315|14 CFR 61.129(a)(4)(i)]]. 150 NM applies only in Hawaii.

quiz.q: A commercial airplane pilot without an instrument rating is prohibited from:
options: Carrying passengers for hire on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night
Any flight for hire at night
Carrying property for hire beyond 50 NM
Flying passengers at night, even for free
quiz.why: The limitation reads: carriage of passengers for hire in airplanes on cross-country flights in excess of 50 NM or at night is prohibited [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(b)(1)]]. It covers passengers for hire only.

quiz.q: Which set of equipment makes an airplane a TAA for commercial training?
options: A GPS and any autopilot
A PFD, an MFD with a GPS moving map, and a two-axis autopilot integrated with nav and heading guidance
Retractable gear, flaps, and a constant-speed propeller
An engine of more than 200 HP and a glass panel
quiz.why: A TAA needs an electronic PFD, an MFD with a GPS moving map, and a two-axis autopilot integrated with the navigation and heading guidance, all continuously visible [[60:321|14 CFR 61.129(j)]]. Gear, flaps and prop define a complex airplane [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]].

quiz.q: A second-class medical is good for commercial privileges until the end of the:
options: 6th month after the exam month
24th month after the exam month
12th month after the exam month, at any age
12th month if under 40, 6th month if 40 or older
quiz.why: For a commercial pilot certificate, a second-class medical expires at the end of the last day of the 12th month after the exam month, at any age [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]].

quiz.q: A commercial pilot flying under BasicMed may:
options: Fly for hire if the airplane has 6 seats or fewer
Fly a paid banner tow below 18,000 ft MSL
Act as PIC for hire on day VFR flights only
Fly only the kind of flights a private pilot may fly
quiz.why: BasicMed does not apply to commercial or ATP privileges; those need a first- or second-class medical [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]]. BasicMed is written for private (and student, recreational, instructor) privileges [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]].

quiz.q: Under 91.147, an operator conducts passenger flights for hire that are:
options: Nonstop, begin and end at the same airport, within 25 statute miles
Any VFR flight under 50 NM
Day VFR flights to any airport within 100 NM
Flights for a charity, up to 4 events a year
quiz.why: 91.147 defines the operator's flights as nonstop passenger flights for hire that begin and end at the same airport within a 25-statute-mile radius [[60:463|14 CFR 91.147(a)]]. Charity events are 91.146.

quiz.q: Who may endorse a student's logbook for solo flight?
options: Any commercial pilot
Any pilot with 250 hours
Only a flight instructor with the appropriate rating (with narrow exceptions)
Any instrument-rated commercial pilot
quiz.why: Except as listed in 61.3(d)(3), only a flight instructor with the appropriate rating may give solo training or endorse a logbook for solo privileges [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(d)(2)]].

quiz.q: According to the RMH, when should you change your personal minimums?
options: On the day of a flight, if the client really needs to go
When you have time for honest self-analysis, not under pressure to fly
Never; personal minimums are set once
After every flight review
quiz.why: Do not adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight. Consider changes when time and objectivity allow an honest self-analysis [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

takeaways: Commercial needs age 18, a private certificate, 250 hours and the 61.129 items, including 10 hours in a complex, turbine or TAA airplane.
Your certificate lets you be paid as a pilot; the operation still needs the right authority (operator certificate, 91.147 LOA, or a 91.146 event).
No instrument rating means no passengers for hire on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night.
Second class covers commercial privileges for 12 calendar months, then steps down to private privileges. BasicMed never covers paid flying.
Currency rules are the same as private; your checkride counts as a flight review.
Complex and high-performance need endorsements; a TAA needs a good checkout. Moving down in performance is risky too.
Paying customers add external pressure. Raise personal minimums, never lower them on the day.
cfi_notes: PHAK 1-18 says commercial pilots without an instrument rating are "restricted to daytime flight within 50 NM when flying for hire." That is broader than the rule. 14 CFR 61.133(b)(1) limits only carrying passengers for hire on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night. Teach the regulation.

PHAK 1-18 says a specific number of complex hours is required and part of the checkride is in a complex airplane. Current 14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(ii) allows complex, turbine or TAA time. Teach the regulation and confirm the airplane needs of your DPE.

The most common commercial-level error: thinking the certificate makes the pilot an operator. Drill "who is the operator, and what authority do they hold?" with job offers (tours, ferry, banner tow, charter for a friend).
Drill the medical step-down with several ages and exam months. Students often think a 13-month-old second-class medical is useless; it is often still good for private flying.

Examiners often probe: the exact 61.133(b) wording, 91.146 vs 91.147, the 500-hour rule for private pilots in 91.146 (not for commercial pilots), BasicMed and pay, and that a commercial pilot needs a CFI certificate to instruct.

AC 68-1A (2017) BasicMed limits (6 occupants, 6,000 lb, 5 passengers) are outdated; 14 CFR 61.113(i) now says 7, 12,500 lb, 6. Its point that BasicMed does not cover commercial privileges still stands.
PHAK 17-2 says a second-class medical is "valid for 1 year." The rule runs it to the end of the 12th month after the exam month (61.23(d)(2)(i)). Make students count calendar months.
Use the scenario to make the student state personal minimums for paid flights out loud, and to separate legal from proficient.
gaps: 14 CFR Part 119 (including the full 119.1(e) list of exceptions), Part 135 and Part 136 are not in the uploaded CFR file. The lesson teaches commercial operations from 14 CFR 1.1, 61.133, 61.3(a)(1)(v), 91.146 and 91.147 instead. The 119.1(e) list itself should be added from the eCFR.

FAA guidance on common carriage versus private carriage and holding out (AC 120-12A and Chief Counsel interpretations) is not in the sources; holding out is shown only through the 93.303 air tour factor.
Part 135 pilot experience minimums (PIC hours for VFR and IFR charter) are not in the sources.
Sample endorsement wording (AC 61-65) for complex, high-performance and flight reviews is not included.
Aircraft-specific transition items (POH/AFM, specific avionics) depend on the training airplane and are not covered by these sources.

activities.title: How many hours to go?
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You trained under Part 61, not Part 142. You have logged 255 hours total, and 60 of them were in a flight training device with an instructor. How many more hours must you log to reach the 250-hour total?
items.why: Only 50 device hours may count outside Part 142 [[60:320|14 CFR 61.129(i)(1)(i)]]. Credit = 255 - 60 + 50 = 245 hours. 250 - 245 = 5 more hours [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)]].

items.q: You have 38 hours of PIC cross-country time. How many more hours of PIC cross-country do you need?
items.why: The rule needs 50 hours of PIC cross-country [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)(2)(ii)]]. 50 - 38 = 12 hours.

items.q: Toward the night VFR requirement for solo or PIC duties, you have logged 3.2 hours in a single-engine airplane. How many more hours do you need?
items.why: The rule needs 5 hours in night VFR conditions [[60:315|14 CFR 61.129(a)(4)(ii)]]. 5.0 - 3.2 = 1.8 hours.

items.q: On those night flights you made 6 takeoffs and 6 landings at an airport with an operating control tower. How many more takeoffs and landings (each) do you need?
items.why: The rule needs 10 takeoffs and 10 landings at a towered airport, each with a traffic pattern [[60:315|14 CFR 61.129(a)(4)(ii)]]. 10 - 6 = 4.

activities.title: Name the parts of a TAA panel
activities.intro: A TAA's PFD must show six instruments, and it needs an MFD too. Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.title: Does the no-instrument limitation stop it?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs. You are a commercial pilot with no instrument rating. Look only at the 61.133(b) limitation.

items.t: Paid passenger on a 40 NM cross-country in daylight
A friend rides along for free on a night flight
Paid ferry flight alone at night, 300 NM
Paid sightseeing ride in daylight, staying within 10 NM
Paid passengers on a 120 NM trip in daylight
Paid passenger on a 15-minute local flight at night
Paid passengers on a 60 NM cross-country at noon

activities.title: Pilot or operator? Match the terms
activities.intro: Tap a term, then tap what it means.

pairs.r: Carries persons or property for hire as a business, not as an air carrier
What a 91.147 nonstop tour operator gets from Flight Standards
Day VFR fundraiser flight for a charity, nonprofit or community cause
Offering to the public to fly for compensation or hire
Is the flying a side part of a business, or the business itself?
Needed to give solo training and endorse training in logbooks

activities.title: Follow a second-class medical as it steps down
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check. You are 45 at your exam.
steps: Through March 31, 2027: good for commercial privileges
Through March 31, 2028: still good for private privileges
April 1, 2028: new medical or BasicMed needed to act as PIC

activities.title: True or false: medical, documents and BasicMed
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A commercial pilot on BasicMed may fly a paid aerial photo flight.
cards.why: No. BasicMed does not apply to commercial pilot privileges; they need a first- or second-class medical [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]].

cards.s: You need only a third-class medical to take the commercial practical test.
cards.why: Yes. A third-class medical is enough when taking a practical test for a commercial certificate [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)(iii)]].

cards.s: Passing the commercial checkride counts as a flight review.
cards.why: Yes. A practical test for a pilot certificate or rating counts [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)(1)]].

cards.s: A commercial pilot must carry the logbook on every flight for hire.
cards.why: No. You must present it on reasonable request [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]]. The carry rules in 61.51(i) are for student, sport and recreational pilots [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(2)-(4)]].

cards.s: A DUI conviction must be reported in writing to the FAA within 60 days.
cards.why: Yes. Each motor vehicle action must be reported within 60 days [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]].

cards.s: Your commercial certificate expires if you do not fly for 24 months.
cards.why: No. Pilot certificates are issued without an expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(c)(1)]]. Your flight review lapses, not the certificate [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]].

activities.title: Your first day as a tour pilot
activities.intro: You are a new commercial pilot, instrument rated, hired by a tour operator that holds a 91.147 Letter of Authorization. You will fly nonstop tours from your home airport in its Cessna 182: 230 HP, fixed gear, glass panel and autopilot. You have never flown it.

steps.s: The chief pilot says: "You're commercial and current. Just go fly the first tour." What do you do?
options: Fly the tour; your commercial certificate covers it
Get ground and flight training and a high-performance endorsement first, plus a checkout on the avionics
Fly one solo lap first, then carry passengers
Have a passenger who is a pilot ride up front
steps.why: 230 HP is more than 200 HP, so you need training and a one-time high-performance endorsement to act as PIC [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]. The FAA also strongly recommends an evaluation from an instructor who knows that airplane's automation [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.1]].

steps.s: You get the endorsement. On the morning of your first tour you check your wallet: your second-class medical exam was 13 months ago. What now?
options: Fly; the medical is still good for private privileges
Fly under BasicMed instead
Fly, but carry no more than 3 passengers
Do not fly tours until you get a new second-class (or first-class) medical
steps.why: For commercial privileges a second-class medical ends after the 12th month after the exam month [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]]. BasicMed does not cover commercial privileges [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]].

steps.s: New medical in hand, you fly a tour. Near another airplane, the autopilot starts an unexpected turn. What do you do?
options: Reduce the level of automation and hand-fly, then sort it out
Reprogram the GPS while the autopilot keeps flying
Turn on more autopilot modes to regain control
Ask a passenger to read the manual to you
steps.why: If the automation is not doing what you expect, reduce the level of automation, fly manually, and take time to resolve it [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

steps.s: After landing, a tour customer offers you $400 to fly her family 120 NM to another city for dinner, right now, in the same airplane.
options: Accept; you are commercial and the operator has an LOA
Accept if she pays only the fuel
Decline; the LOA covers only nonstop flights from this airport within 25 statute miles
Accept, but file an IFR flight plan
steps.why: A 91.147 LOA covers nonstop passenger flights that begin and end at the same airport within 25 statute miles [[60:463|14 CFR 91.147(a)]]. A trip to another city is a different operation, and you must be qualified under the parts that apply to it [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]].

steps.s: Last tour of the day: the wind is now gusting right at your personal crosswind minimum, and six people are waiting. What do you do?
options: Go; the airplane's demonstrated crosswind is higher
Delay or cancel; do not lower your minimums under pressure
Lower your minimum by 5 knots just this once
Go, but tell the passengers to expect a bumpy landing
steps.why: Waiting customers are an external pressure [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Never adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: For the day cross-country with an instructor, you fly 2.1 hours to an airport 95 NM straight-line from home and back. Does it meet 61.129(a)(3)(iii)?
options: Yes, because it lasted more than 2 hours
Yes, because the round trip is 190 NM
No, the straight-line distance must be more than 100 NM from the departure point
No, it must be flown solo
final_quiz.why: The flight needs 2 hours and a total straight-line distance of more than 100 NM from the original point of departure [[60:315|14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(iii)]]. It is flown with an instructor as part of the training hours [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: You trained under Part 61 and logged 70 hours in a flight training device with an instructor. How many of them can count toward the 250-hour total?
final_quiz.why: Outside a Part 142 course, the maximum is 50 hours, from an authorized instructor in a simulator or FTD that represents the class of airplane [[60:320|14 CFR 61.129(i)(1)(i)]]. 100 is the Part 142 limit [[60:320|61.129(i)(2)(i)]].

final_quiz.q: You are 36 and had a second-class exam in January 2026. On March 10, 2027, which flight may you act as PIC of?
options: A paid aerial photo flight
A personal flight with a friend, no pay involved
A paid ferry flight with no passengers
A paid tour flight for a 91.147 operator
final_quiz.why: For commercial privileges the medical ended January 31, 2027 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(i)]]. For private privileges (under 40 at the exam) it runs through January 31, 2031 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)(ii)]]. Every paid flight uses commercial privileges.

final_quiz.q: Your commercial certificate has the no-instrument limitation. Which flight does that limitation prohibit?
options: A free flight with a friend at night
A paid ferry flight alone at night
A paid passenger on a 20 NM local flight in daylight
A paid passenger on a 75 NM cross-country in daylight
final_quiz.why: The limitation prohibits carrying passengers for hire on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(b)(1)]]. A 75 NM paid passenger trip is over 50 NM.

final_quiz.q: A fixed-gear trainer has a 180 HP engine, a PFD, an MFD with a GPS moving map, and a two-axis autopilot integrated with nav and heading guidance. Which is true?
options: You need a complex endorsement to act as PIC
You need a high-performance endorsement to act as PIC
It cannot be used for any of the 10 hours of advanced training
It counts as a TAA for training, and no 61.31 endorsement is required
final_quiz.why: It meets the TAA equipment list [[60:321|14 CFR 61.129(j)]], so it counts toward the 10 hours [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(ii)]]. It is not complex (fixed gear) [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]] and not high-performance (not more than 200 HP) [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]].

final_quiz.q: You are rated ASEL and fly a training cross-country as sole manipulator with your instructor on board. How may you log it?
options: As PIC time and as training received
As solo time
As training only; PIC needs you to be alone
As SIC time
final_quiz.why: A rated pilot who is sole manipulator may log PIC [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(e)(1)(i)]], and the lesson is logged as training from an authorized instructor [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(2)(iv)]]. Solo is only when you are the sole occupant [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(d)]].

final_quiz.q: A new commercial pilot posts online: "I'll fly you anywhere in my rented plane, $200 an hour." What is the core problem?
options: Only the hourly rate; pro rata sharing would be fine
He is offering carriage for hire to the public, which is an operator's business, not just a pilot privilege
Commercial pilots may not advertise at all
The flights must be under 50 NM
final_quiz.why: Holding out to the public is a sign of a commercial operation [[60:693|14 CFR 93.303]]. Carrying persons for compensation as a major enterprise for profit makes him a commercial operator [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]], and his certificate covers only flights where he is qualified under the parts that apply to the operation [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Which condition applies to a 91.146 charity event passenger flight?
options: It may be flown at night with an instrument rating
It may go to any airport within 50 NM
It must be day VFR, nonstop, and begin and end at the same airport within 25 statute miles
The pilot must hold an ATP certificate
final_quiz.why: The flight must be nonstop, begin and end at the same airport within a 25-statute-mile radius, and be flown in day VFR [[60:462|14 CFR 91.146(b)(1), (6)]]. A private pilot PIC needs 500 hours [[60:462|91.146(b)(9)]].

final_quiz.q: Your last 6 approaches, holding and tracking were done in April 2026. Today is October 20, 2026. May you act as PIC under IFR today?
options: No, it ran out on October 1
No, you need an instrument proficiency check
Yes, but only with a safety pilot
Yes, you are current through October 31, 2026
final_quiz.why: The tasks must be within the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. For an October flight that is April through September, so April counts. An IPC is needed only after more than six more calendar months [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: You were convicted of a DUI. What must you do with the FAA?
options: Report it in writing within 60 days
Tell your AME at your next exam only
Nothing unless you are flying for hire
Report it within 10 days by phone
final_quiz.why: Each motor vehicle action must be reported in writing to the FAA Civil Aviation Security Division within 60 days [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]]. Not reporting is grounds for suspension or revocation [[60:202|61.15(f)]].

final_quiz.q: You trained in a glass-cockpit TAA. Your first job is in an older, slower airplane with analog gauges. What does AC 90-109A say?
options: Moving to a simpler airplane needs no training
Only the POH needs review
Moving down has as many challenges as moving up; avionics may be less capable and weather affects it more
Training is needed only for retractable gear
final_quiz.why: There are just as many challenges moving from high- to low-performance airplanes: weather and headwinds affect them more, crosswind ability may be lower, and avionics may be less capable [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10, 2]].

final_quiz.q: A client is paying for a trip and wants to leave now. The ceiling is just below your written personal minimum. What is the best choice?
options: Lower your minimum a little, since you are current
Go, and turn back if it gets worse
Go if the client signs a waiver
Keep your minimum and delay; client pressure is an external pressure hazard
final_quiz.why: External pressures can make pilots ignore other hazards [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Do not adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: For a paid flight, you carry your commercial certificate, your passport and a third-class medical from last month. Are your documents complete?
options: Yes, all three are present
No, commercial privileges need at least a second-class medical
No, a passport is not an accepted photo ID
Yes, if your logbook is also on board
final_quiz.why: You need the pilot certificate, a photo ID and the appropriate medical [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]], [[60:189|61.3(c)(1)]]. For commercial privileges that is at least a second-class medical [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)(ii)]]. A passport is an accepted photo ID [[60:188|61.3(a)(2)(iv)]].

final_quiz.q: You passed your commercial checkride on March 12, 2026. With no other review, what is the last day you may act as PIC?
options: March 12, 2028
March 31, 2027
March 31, 2028
February 28, 2028
final_quiz.why: A practical test counts as a flight review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)(1)]]. The review period runs from the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month you fly, so March 2026 covers you through March 31, 2028 [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]].
